notes.meaning: Nebuchadnezzar arrived at Jerusalem in the middle of winter to begin a total siege. The Babylonian army surrounded the city so no food or help could enter, just as Jeremiah had long warned.

After eighteen long months of starvation, the Babylonian soldiers smashed through the thick stone walls. The fall of the city proved that Jeremiah spoke God's truth while the flattering prophets were wrong.

The Babylonian commanders entered Jerusalem and sat down at the Middle Gate. In ancient times, rulers held court and conducted business at city gates, so sitting there showed they were now in complete control of the city.

When King Zedekiah saw the enemy generals inside the walls, he and his soldiers fled into the night. They slipped out through a southern gate near the royal garden, abandoning the people to escape toward the Jordan valley.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note that verses 4–13 are omitted from the earliest Greek translation of Jeremiah (the Septuagint), suggesting that this section was later added from parallel accounts in Jeremiah 52 or 2 Kings 25.

notes.meaning: Babylonian soldiers chased after Zedekiah and caught him on the plains near Jericho. They hauled him north to Riblah, where Nebuchadnezzar put him on trial like a criminal for breaking his oath of loyalty.

At Riblah, Nebuchadnezzar murdered Zedekiah's young sons right before his eyes, along with the leading officials of Judah. Zedekiah had repeatedly refused God's command to surrender, and his stubbornness brought ruin to his entire house.

Nebuchadnezzar gouged out Zedekiah's eyes and bound him in bronze chains to drag him off to Babylon. This exact cruelty fulfilled two prophecies that seemed to contradict each other: Zedekiah looked upon the king of Babylon face to face, yet he never saw the city of Babylon because he arrived there blind.

The Babylonian troops tore down the defensive walls of Jerusalem and set fire to the royal palace and the people's homes. The proud city was reduced to ashes, showing that God's warnings through Jeremiah were true.

The captain of the guard gathered the surviving residents and those who had already surrendered, marching them away into exile. The captives were led off in chains to Babylon, leaving the city empty and ruined.

The Babylonians left behind only the poorest people, who had never owned any property, and gave them fields and vineyards. While Babylon did this so the land would stay productive, God showed His justice by giving homes to the oppressed.

Nebuchadnezzar commanded his chief officer to locate Jeremiah, protect him from any harm, and provide whatever he requested. The Babylonian king had likely heard about the prophet's advice to surrender, but God was the one directing the foreign ruler to keep His servant safe.

Babylon's highest officers pulled Jeremiah out of the prison courtyard and placed him in the care of Gedaliah. Gedaliah came from a godly family that had protected Jeremiah in the past, and this allowed the prophet to live in safety among his own people.

This part of the story looks back to the time before Jerusalem fell, while Jeremiah was still locked in the palace courtyard. God had given Jeremiah a special message of comfort for Ebed-melech, the official who had boldly pulled the prophet out of the muddy pit.

God sent Jeremiah to tell Ebed-melech that the warnings of destruction against Jerusalem were about to come true before his very eyes. Even as judgment fell upon the unfaithful city, God showed that He had not forgotten this faithful foreigner.

The LORD promised to shield Ebed-melech from being captured by the royal officials he feared. Ebed-melech had risked his life to rescue Jeremiah, and God answered his natural fears with a promise of personal safety.

God promised that Ebed-melech would survive the coming slaughter and escape with his life as a prize of war. He was delivered not simply because he was brave, but because he put his trust in the Lord.
